When you first fall in love, your heart pounds just from holding hands. But as time passes, even couples who used to phone each other every day get in touch less, and there are more days when they quarrel over small things. So some people think their love has cooled and break up. But this is not the end of love — it is a move to the next stage. Here are some ways to love for a long time.

First, listen to what the other person says to the end. Listening often gives more strength than advice.
Second, say thank you even for small things. Unless you say it, the other person cannot know how you feel.
Third, when you quarrel, talk only about the present problem. If you bring up old matters again, the anger does not go away.
Fourth, respect each other's time alone too. You do not always have to be together.
Fifth, now and then go on a date as you did when you first met. Going back to a restaurant you used to go to is a good idea too.

Love does not keep itself. To spend your whole lives together, both of you have to make an effort.

Hello. I am an office worker who has been married for ten years. Today I am writing because I want to tell the story of my wife and me.

My wife was someone who worked in a small bakery in the city where I was studying abroad. Every morning I went to that bakery and bought bread. In truth I went to see her rather than for the bread. But I was due to return to Korea a year later, so I didn't have the courage to confess.

The day before I went home, I went to the bakery for the last time. But my wife gave me a letter first. It said, ‘If the customer who used to come every day stops coming, I think I shall miss him very much.’ That day I told her my feelings for the first time.

For three years after that, we dated far apart. At first my parents worried because our nationalities were different. But after meeting my wife in person, they liked her very much and said she was kind-hearted.

Even now, my wife bakes the bread she used to make back then every weekend. When I smell that bread, I remember the days when we first met.

**-던** describes a noun by something the speaker **remembers from the past**. Two uses. ① An action that was **in progress and left unfinished**: 제가 읽**던** 신문 (the newspaper I was reading — I haven't finished it). ② Something that happened **repeatedly or for a while** in the past: 아버지가 타시**던** 차 (the car my father used to drive), 자주 걷**던** 길.

**-(으)ㄴ** = a single completed action: 어제 **먹은** 빵 (the bread I ate yesterday — it's gone). **-던** = not finished, or habitual: **먹던** 빵 (the bread I was eating — some is left). With adjectives -던 recalls a past state that has changed: 어제까지 따뜻하**던** 날씨가 추워졌어요.

Three nouns, three degrees of firmness. **생각** = I'm thinking of, I intend to. **계획** = I have a plan. **예정** = it is scheduled (formal, fixed). Form: V + **(으)ㄹ** + noun + 이다: 올해는 담배를 **끊을 생각이에요**. 봄에 이사**할 계획이에요**. 회의는 두 시에 시작**될 예정입니다**.
ㄹ-stems: 살다 → **살** 생각, 만들다 → **만들** 계획. 듣다 → **들을** 생각. Negative intention: 결혼**하지 않을** 생각이에요. Asking: 언제쯤 취직**할 생각이에요?** 아이는 몇 명 **낳을 계획이에요?**
V-(으)려면 (아직) 멀었다 — a long way from

-(으)려면 (“if one is to…”) + 멀었다 (“it is far”): a lot of time or effort is still needed. 한국말을 잘하**려면** 아직 **멀었어요** (I'm still a long way from speaking Korean well). 졸업하**려면 멀었어요**. It is always in the past form **멀었다**, even though the meaning is present.
It is the standard modest reply to praise: 한국말을 정말 잘하시네요. — 아니에요, 잘하**려면 아직 멀었어요**. Usually a reason follows: 배운 지 석 달밖에 안 됐거든요.

When people first join a company, everyone wants to do their work well. But nobody is good at everything from the start. From ten years of experience training new employees, I will tell you three things.

1. If you don't know, ask.
The biggest mistake new employees make is pretending to know what they don't. If you worry alone and then do the work wrongly, more time is needed later. Asking is nothing to be ashamed of. Only, be sure to note down what you hear so that you don't ask the same question twice.

2. Do your best in small things.
At first you are given small jobs such as photocopying or sorting papers. To the person who does such jobs meticulously, a boss entrusts more important work. No company entrusts big work to someone who does small things carelessly.

3. Greet people first.
Work is not something you do alone. A person who greets others cheerfully every morning has many colleagues who help when help is needed. Skill comes with time, but attitude shows from the first day.

If life at work is hard for you now, try putting just one of these three into practice first.

About how many hours a day do you spend sitting? We sit when we work at the office and when we look at our phones at home. The best way is to get up and walk often. But on busy days even that isn't easy. So here is some simple stretching you can do on a chair.

Second, put both hands on your waist and open your chest out. Lean back a little and come back.
Third, turn your head slowly to the right and then to the left.

Many foreigners who are invited to a wedding or a funeral in Korea wonder what they should wear. There are no rules that must be obeyed, but there is some etiquette that is good to know.

When you go to a wedding, you dress up neatly. Men usually wear a suit, and women often wear a dress or formal clothes. That day the bride should stand out most, so it is better for guests to avoid a white dress. People don't usually wear very showy clothes either. Instead of a present, many people give gift money in an envelope.

When you go to a funeral, you wear black or dark clothes. You don't wear a bright tie or showy earrings. If you have to go suddenly from work and have no black clothes, dark everyday clothes are all right.

At relaxed occasions such as a housewarming or a birthday gathering, you may wear everyday clothes. When you don't know what to wear, ask the person you are going with in advance. More important than what you wear is the wish to congratulate or to comfort.

On the roof of our block of flats there is a small vegetable patch. Until three years ago it was an empty roof where nobody went up. But an old lady who lives on the eighth floor filled a few boxes with soil and began to plant lettuce.

At first nobody showed any interest. But the children who saw the lettuce growing were fascinated and went up to the roof every day. The parents who followed them also brought boxes, one after another. Now more than twenty households grow chillies, tomatoes and aubergines.

Vegetables are not the only thing that has changed since the patch appeared. Neighbours who used not to greet each other even when they met in the lift now call each other by name. She says that the more you farm, the more there is to learn. On the roof I learnt that in the city too, the more you tend your neighbours, the closer you become.

It's been a long time. Last week I went to the neighbourhood where we grew up together, for the first time in thirty years. It had changed so much that when I got off the bus I thought I had come to a different city.

Do you remember the playing field where we played football every day? There is now a big library on that spot. There is a garden on the roof, and a robot finds the books for you. By the stream where we swam every summer there is now a cycle path, and all the cars run underground, so the streets are quiet.

There were many curious things too. The shops have no shopkeepers, and people watch the news through their glasses as they walk. It is convenient, but somehow they looked a little lonely.

The adjective takes **이/가**; the new verb takes **을/를**: 저는 고향**이** 그리워요 → 아버지는 고향**을** 그리워하세요. 저는 벌레**가** 싫어요 → 언니는 벌레**를** 싫어해요.

I have lived on my own for three years. For the first year, even when my salary came in, no money was left in my account. I didn't think I was wasting money, so it was strange. So for three months I wrote down everything I spent. Here are four habits I changed after that.

First, I checked the money that goes out automatically every month. The subscriptions for a video service I didn't watch and apps I didn't use came to as much as thirty thousand won a month. I cancelled them at once.

Second, before going shopping for food, I take a photo of my fridge. I buy things I already have less often, and I throw away less food.

Third, I don't drop into the convenience shop on my way home from work. If you drop in when you're hungry, you end up buying even things you don't need.

Fourth, on pay day I first send the money I mean to save to a different account. This is because if you try to save what is left, nothing is left.

Halfway up the hill there is a broad, flat rock. People sit there and listen to the sounds in silence for twenty minutes. In the old days, Koreans did not throw away the scraps of cloth left over from making clothes. They joined the small pieces one by one to make cloths for wrapping or covering things, and such a cloth is called a jogakbo.

Because leftover cloth is used, the pieces all differ in size and colour. Triangular pieces, square pieces and diamond-shaped pieces come together and naturally form a pattern. No two jogakbo in the world are the same.

A jogakbo was used in many ways. It was used for wrapping presents, for covering a table laid with food, and for hanging at a window to keep out the sun. When not in use, it folded down to the size of a palm, so it was easy to store.

These days many people hang a jogakbo on the wall like a picture. Looking closely, you can see how meticulous the needlework is. The spirit of people long ago, who tried to throw nothing away, is now loved as beautiful design. If you go to a museum, it is worth looking for one.

This happened last month. In the school corridor I met Eunho, a friend from my class. I waved gladly, but Eunho pretended not to see me and just walked past. I was startled. I remembered that the day before I had spoken frankly about Eunho's presentation. ‘He must be angry because of what I said.’

From that day I too pretended not to know Eunho when I saw him. I ate lunch with other friends too. A few days later there was even a rumour that we had had a big quarrel. In fact we hadn't said a single word to each other.

After about a week, Eunho came to find me first. “Why are you avoiding me these days? What have I done wrong?” I told him what had happened in the corridor. Eunho thought for a long while and then began to laugh. “My glasses broke that morning and I couldn't see a thing. I didn't even know you'd waved.”

Now that I heard it, Eunho really hadn't been wearing glasses that day. I blushed. Because of a misunderstanding that could have been cleared up in a minute by asking, I had spent a hard week. That day we made up and went to eat tteokbokki together. Since then, when something odd happens, I don't brood on it alone — I ask directly.

There are stories that many people believe but that are not true. Today let's look at three that have to do with Korea.

First, ‘All kimchi is spicy.’ Not all kimchi is spicy. White kimchi and dongchimi have no chilli powder in them, so they are not spicy at all. People who can't eat spicy food, and children, eat them happily.

Second, ‘You catch a cold when it is cold.’ A cold is caught not from the cold but from a virus. It is said that colds are common in winter because people shut their doors and gather indoors, so viruses spread easily. So dressing warmly is good, but washing your hands often matters more.

Third, ‘Every Korean can do taekwondo.’ Not every Korean is good at taekwondo. Many children learn it at an academy when they are small, but most forget it when they grow up.

When people first hear such things, many are surprised: “That isn't true?” Not everything is right just because many people say it. Before believing, let's check once more.

**아니 땐 굴뚝에 연기 날까** — “would smoke rise from a chimney with no fire lit?”: there is a reason behind every rumour (no smoke without fire). **낮말은 새가 듣고 밤말은 쥐가 듣는다** — “birds hear what is said by day, mice what is said by night”: secrets get out, so mind what you say. **발 없는 말이 천 리 간다** — “words without feet travel a thousand ri”: talk spreads far and fast.

Korean is read in **sense groups**. Pause after the topic or subject (…은/는, …이/가), after a time or place phrase, and before a long object or the final verb: 오늘은 전국적으로 / 가을비가 내리겠습니다. 저는 지난달에 / 학교 복도에서 / 친구를 만났습니다. Don't pause between a modifier and its noun (제가 **다녔던 학교**).

[Act 1. Night, the kitchen] The light is off. Father comes in quietly and opens the fridge door.

Father: (startled) Oh dear, I've gone and eaten half of it! What am I to do? (He hides the cake behind the kimchi box and goes out.)

[Act 2. Morning, the living room] Mother rushes in carrying an empty plate.

Son: (jumping up) It wasn't me!
Mother: You're the only one who went to the kitchen last night.
Son: I only drank water, I'm telling you! Really. I didn't even know there was a cake.
Daughter: (turning round sharply) Then is it Dad? Dad, what's that on your mouth?
Father: (shaking his head) This? Oh, it's nothing. It's toothpaste. It's toothpaste, I tell you!
Daughter: Does toothpaste smell of strawberries?
Father: (sighing) I'm sorry. I meant to have just one bite, but before I knew it I'd eaten half.
Mother: Half? There's nothing on the plate but crumbs!
Father: (startled) What? I only ate half, I'm telling you!

[Act 3. The same place] Grandmother comes in slowly.

Grandmother: Why all this noise first thing in the morning?
Daughter: Grandma, somebody ate the whole cake. Dad says he only ate half.
Grandmother: (nodding quietly) The other half… I ate.
All: (startled) What?
Grandmother: I came out at dawn to take my medicine and saw it in the fridge. I tried to resist, but it looked so delicious that I ended up eating it all. I didn't know it was my birthday cake.
(Everyone bursts out laughing.)

[The curtain falls.]

Last Saturday I saw a play called ‘The Vanished Cake’ with a friend in a small theatre in Daehangno. To tell the truth, I don't much like plays. The one I saw at high school was so boring that I ended up dozing off. So this time too, when my friend said let's go, I said I wouldn't. But my friend said, “It's really good, I'm telling you. Trust me just this once,” so I went along.

The theatre was a small place that could seat about fifty. The stage and the seats were close, so we could see even the actors' expressions. The plot is simple. It is the story of a family trying to find out who ate Grandmother's birthday cake.

The scene I remember best was the one where the father says he will have just one bite and ends up eating half. The actor who played the father was really convincing. None of the audience could hold back their laughter. In the last scene, where the grandmother confesses, I too ended up laughing out loud.

There was something lacking too. The actor who played the son forgot his lines once, and for a moment it went quiet. Still, another actor helped him out naturally, so it soon passed.

When the play was over, I clapped louder than anyone. My friend laughed and said, “See? I told you it was good.” We have decided to go and see another play together next month.

A **연극** is performed on a **무대** before the **관객**. The **배우** learn their **대사** from the **대본**, and each plays a **역할**: 아버지 **역할을 하다 / 맡다**. A play is divided into **막** (acts) and **장면** (scenes). At the end the audience **박수를 칩니다**.

Yes: **고개를 끄덕이다** (to nod). No: **고개를 가로젓다** (to shake one's head; ㅅ-irregular: 가로**저어요**, 가로**저으며**). Loud: **소리를 지르다** (to shout; 질러요). Quiet: **속삭이다** (to whisper). Tired or sorry: **한숨을 쉬다** (to sigh).
**벌떡 일어나다** — to spring to one's feet. **홱 돌아보다** — to turn round sharply. **깜짝 놀라다** — to start with surprise. The little words 벌떡, 홱, 깜짝 paint the suddenness; they belong to exactly these verbs.

**들여다보다** — to look into (a box, a mirror, a fridge): 거울을 들여다보다. **숨기다** — to hide something (cf. **숨다**, to hide oneself). **빼앗다** — to snatch away. **깨뜨리다** — to break something ↔ **깨지다** — to get broken: 제가 컵을 **깨뜨렸어요** / 컵이 **깨졌어요**.

You **say again, with force**, something the listener did not believe or did not take in: 재미있**다니까요** (it IS good, I'm telling you). It is the **quoted form + 니까**: “since I say that…”. So it follows the rules of reported speech.
The same works for the other sentence types: a command → **-(으)라니까(요)**: 빨리 오**라니까요**! (come quickly, I tell you!); a suggestion → **-자니까(요)**: 같이 가**자니까** (let's go together, I said).

It often carries **impatience** — “how many times must I say it?” — so be careful with people above you. Between friends it can also simply be lively emphasis: 내 동생은 눈만 뜨면 게임을 **한다니까** (my brother plays games the moment he opens his eyes, honestly).

Unit 17: **-다니요?** — the **listener** is amazed at what was said. Unit 18: **-다니까요** — the **speaker** insists. They often meet: 이게 제 얼굴**이라니요**? — 그렇**다니까요**. (This is my face?! — It is, I'm telling you.)

**결국** (in the end): 결국 포기하고 말았어요. **그만** (before I knew it): 그만 웃고 말았어요. **끝내** (to the last): 끝내 오지 않고 말았다. And a first clause with **-지만 / -았는데 / -(으)려고 했는데**: 참으려고 했는데 다 먹고 말았어요.

**-아/어 버리다** stresses that an action is **completely done** — with relief or regret, and it may be deliberate: 숙제를 다 해 버렸어요 (got it all done). **-고 말다** stresses the **unwanted final result**, usually after resisting: 참다가 결국 화를 내고 말았어요. You cannot use -고 말다 for something you did happily on purpose.
With **-겠-** and a first-person subject the meaning flips to **strong determination**: 이번에는 꼭 합격하**고 말겠어요** (this time I WILL pass). 올해 안에 이 책을 다 읽**고 말 거예요**.

Noun: ~~친구다니까요~~ → 친구**라니까요**; 아니다 → **아니라니까요**. 3. -고 말다 with a happy, intended action: ~~합격하고 말았어요~~ (if you are glad) → 합격**했어요**. 4. Modifier: ~~먹고 말는 장면~~ → 먹고 **마는** 장면. 5. Don't confuse 깨**지다** (it breaks) and 깨**뜨리다** (I break it).
